home_eyebrow: Open research on modern board games
home_q: What does an AI learn when it plays a board game millions of times against itself?
home_lede: We let AI agents learn modern board games only by playing against copies of themselves — nobody teaches them a strategy. Then every finished AI plays thousands of games, and we compare what the winners did differently: which cards, combinations and habits go with winning.
step1: It plays against copies of itself and keeps what wins. Over millions of moves it becomes a strong player.
step2: The finished AI plays 2,000 games with fixed random seeds, so anyone can replay exactly the same games.
step3: Every final board is scored piece by piece. Comparing winners with losers shows what goes with winning.
games_sub: Open a game to see its discoveries, the strategy in plain words, every card and how the AI was trained.
add_text: Anyone can add a game. A coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Grok and others) follows the repository's step-by-step skills: it writes the rules in its own words, builds the card data, the engine and its tests, trains the AI and runs the standard experiments.
add_1: Open a branch and say which game you want, e.g. "add the game Azul".
add_2: The agent works through the skills; every step leaves files you can check.
add_3: Automated checks, a test for every rule and card, and a second review must pass before training.
add_4: Open a pull request; the dashboard updates when it is merged.
trust_h: Why you can trust the numbers
trust_1: Every rule of an engine has an ID and a test; rules and cards are checked against at least two independent sources.
trust_2: Every experiment is a recipe: the same code, model and seed replay the same games. CI replays the first 20 games of every experiment.
trust_3: Every AI has a strength card: paired games against models it never trained against, and against a greedy baseline.
trust_4: Small samples are greyed out and every effect shows its uncertainty.
caveat: These are patterns in the AI's own games: they show what winners have more of, not always why. The AI plays well against an equally strong copy of itself — that is not a proven best strategy.

lift_expl: Effect on winning: how much more often {boards} with it win than the average (in percentage points). Whiskers: ± 2 standard errors.
order_expl: Win rate by seat. The AI rotates through every seat, so differences come from the turn order itself. Bars: difference from an equal share.
items_expl: {n} in total, from {src}. Click one for its profile. Effect on winning = how much more often {boards} with it win than the average.
grey_note: Greyed rows are on fewer than {n} {boards}: their numbers are too noisy to trust.
profile_expl: Players with it win {win} of games (average {base}), on {n} {boards}.
never_on_board: Never ended on a final {boards} in these games.
by_length: Effect on winning by game length
boards_expl: Ten sample games from {src}: the highest, typical and lowest winner scores; points per piece as scored at the end.
action_mix: What the AI does on its turn
score_split_expl: Average points per category and player.
optional_expl: How often the AI uses an optional power when it may.
length_expl: Games last {a} to {b} rounds per player. Longer games give everyone more cards, so effects partly reflect what is possible with more cards.
by_length_expl: Effect on winning in five equal groups of games, shortest to longest. Hollow points: fewer than 30 boards.
compare_expl: The same game learned twice: the original AI (older training method) and the new, stronger AI. Where they disagree, the stronger AI's view is the better guide.
deals_expl: Both AIs played the same {n} deals. Winner's average score: new {new}, original {old}; the new AI's winner scored higher in {share} of deals.
changes_expl: Change in effect on winning (new minus original), only clear changes (more than 2 standard errors).
lab_h: Lab: how the AIs were trained and tested
lab_expl: Everything needed to check and reproduce the numbers: each AI's training recipe and strength, and each experiment's exact recipe.
strength_expl: Paired games on the same deals (each AI plays every seat once). An AI counts as finished when it clearly beats opponents it never trained against and the greedy baseline.
curve_expl: Win rate during training against fixed opponents (paired games every million steps).
exp_expl: Each experiment is a recipe. The first command replays it completely; the second replays the first 20 games and checks them against the stored fingerprint.
training_now_h: The AI is still learning this game
training_now: The rules engine and all {n} {items} are in place and tested; the AI is training. Discoveries appear here once a finished AI has played its 2,000 games.
how_lede: Every number on this site comes from thousands of games an AI played against copies of itself. Here is what the measures mean and how far you can trust them.
how_example: "Gentian: effect on winning +8.6 pp" means: in the AI's games, players who had Gentian in their final forest won 8.6 percentage points more often than an average player (58.6 % instead of 50 % with 2 players). It does not prove Gentian causes the win — maybe winners simply had time to play it — but a big, steady difference over thousands of games is a strong hint.
plan_one_line: The winning plan in one sentence
g_lift_d: How much more (or less) often players win when they have this card, type or habit, compared with the average player. 0 = no difference.
g_pp_d: The difference between two percentages: from 50 % to 58 % is +8 percentage points.
g_err_d: The uncertainty: about 95 % of the time the true value lies within this range. A small effect with a wide range may be chance.
g_edge_d: How many more copies of a card the winner had than the loser of the same game, on average. It compares players in the same game, so luck of the deal and game length cancel out.
g_presence_d: In what share of final boards the card appears at all.
g_points_d: Average points one copy of the card scored at the end.
g_type_d: A simple label for a player's whole board, e.g. the tree symbol or habitat it has most of. Shows which overall plans win.
g_mirror_d: Every seat is played by the same AI, so everyone plays equally well; the differences come from choices and luck, not from a weaker opponent.
g_seed_d: Each game is dealt from a numbered seed. With the same AI and seeds anyone can replay exactly the same games — that is how the numbers can be checked.
g_strength_d: Each AI is tested in games against opponents it never trained against and against a simple greedy player. Only a 'finished' AI is strong enough that its games mean something.
g_grey_d: Cards that appeared too rarely for their numbers to be trusted.
g_corr_d: The site shows what winners have more of. Whether that is why they won is a judgement — the written notes try to make it, carefully.
